cards.explanation: The answer is kill. That's the word the text uses: Ishbi-benob resolved to kill David. I think a worn-out king is the last person who should be on that man's list, friends. The text says David became exhausted just before this.

The answer is Abishai son of Zeruiah. He comes to David's aid, strikes the Philistine and kills him. The text gives us no more about him here. I think David was mighty glad to see him show up, friends, because a tired man can only duck so fast.

The answer is that David must never go to battle with them again. David's men swear, "You must never again go out with us to battle…" It's a firm line, and I bet it came out of a very tense moment. They swear it, and that tells me they mean it.

The answer is True. The text says Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. That's the same family line as Ishbi-benob. Rapha's descendants keep turning up in these battles, friends.

The answer is Goliath the Gittite. Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite kills his brother at Gob. Goliath is the famous Philistine champion from Gath whom David struck down (1 Samuel 17:4, 50). So this brother has a very big name hanging over him, bakers.

The answer is False. The text never mentions bronze armor on this man. It says he had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. That's the detail the text gives about him, friends.

The answer is Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimei. When the man at Gath taunts Israel, Jonathan kills him. So this Jonathan is David's nephew. A taunt is a risky thing to say to Israel, bakers, and here it's the last thing that man says.

The answer is four. The text sums it up: "So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants." Count them with me, friends: Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath's brother and the man with twenty-four fingers and toes. It all adds up.
